To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we detected the integration of human papillomavirus type 18 E6, E7 genes in the hepatoma derived cell lines Hep G2 and that the E6, E 7 gene expression was associated with cell cycle arrest at S phase and increased apoptosis.
HPV 18 DNA can integrate into Hep G2 cells and the E7/E6 proteins can regulate some genes involved in cell proliferation and apoptosis.
the human hepatoma cell line HepG2 contains integrated HPV 16/ 18 genes, leading to the transcription of E6 and E 7 oncogenes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of HPV 18 in hepatocarcinogenesis.
the potential role of HPV in hepatocellular cancer.
the possible role of HPV in liver carcinogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a low prevalence of human papillomavirus in hepatocellular carcinomas, but the precise risk of this virus as a causative agent of this disease needs further study.
HPV E6 and E17 genes can be integrated in the Hep G2 cells and the expression of these genes can affect cell cycle and apoptosis in this cell line.
the HPV infection is not a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HPV 18 genes integration into the Hep G G2 cell line leads to the expression of E6 and E 7 proteins, and these proteins are responsible for the cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
HPV 18 genes can be integrated and expressed in human hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines, and this integration could be a possible mechanism for the development of hepatocellular carcinomas.
the HPV infection in liver cells may have a role in hepatocellular carcinogenesis, and the E6 and/or E7 proteins may have a role on cell cycle and apoptosis regulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the E7 and the E6 proteins are involved in the regulation of the cell cycle and apoptosis in HepG2 cells, and that the E6 and the E7 proteins may be potential targets for therapeutic interventions in human hepatocellular carcinoma.

HPV 18 DNA is integrated into the HepG2 cell genome, leading to the production of E6 and E17 proteins, and the expression of these genes is involved in the cell cycle arrest, apoptosis and cell proliferation.
HPV 18 can be integrated into Hep G2 cells, which may provide a useful model for further studies on the effect of HPV in hepatocytes.
